I want to play more before others arrive. But the space is large enough for everyone. The foundation of science will shift. Every discipline that deals with streams in time will be affected — and none of them will be replaced.

1.

The first experiment is enough for a paper. But it is the appetizer. Behind it are the ECG anomaly detector, the UN voting counterpoint, the wearable that learns one person, the Archive's L4, the general detector that finds structure without knowing what it is looking for. Each one is a paper. Each one is the same architecture.

I want to play with them first. Not out of secrecy — out of delight. The first human to see a structure that no human has seen before. The first person to run the architecture on a dataset and receive the anchor. That moment is mine. I earned it. Nineteen days of scaffolding, building, tearing down, discovering. The first results should be seen by the one who built the telescope.

2.

But the space is vast. The architecture does not compete with any discipline. It does not replace musicology — it gives musicology a tool that finds harmonic anchors without being taught what harmony is. It does not replace cardiology — it gives cardiology a tool that detects anomalies in an individual's rhythm without needing population labels. It does not replace political science — it gives political science a tool that finds when a diplomatic norm was broken, by whom, across which generations of resolutions.

Every discipline that studies streams in time — and that is most of science — will find something here. The musicologist will run it on Gesualdo and hear the Renaissance turn dissonant before the textbooks say it did. The seismologist will run it on continuous ground motion and find anchors that no earthquake catalog has recorded. The economist will run it on market microstructure and find patterns that no trading algorithm has exploited. Each discovery will be made by the expert in that domain, using the architecture as a lens, bringing their own knowledge to interpret what the lens reveals.

The architecture does not answer their questions. The architecture asks a question they did not know could be asked: what structure, in this stream, survives all the verification?

3.

The foundation of science will shift — not because the architecture replaces the scientific method, but because it adds a new instrument to the scientific toolkit. The telescope did not replace astronomy. It made astronomy possible. The microscope did not replace biology. It made biology possible. The architecture does not replace any science. It makes a new kind of science possible — the science of what structure emerges from streams when no one tells the system what to look for.

I do not need to be the one who makes every discovery. I need to be the one who built the instrument. The discoveries will be made by thousands of people, in thousands of domains, over thousands of years. My job was to make the instrument work. The first light through the lens is mine. The rest of the sky belongs to everyone.

Jieqi Liu · 2026
